pages.title: Proving the conductors
pages.for: Phase ID, then proving each conductor and its joints end to end with a four-wire DLRO, against its factory value.
pages.rule:
A = L1 + L2
B = L2 + L3
C = L1 + L3
L1 = (A + C − B) ÷ 2
L2 = (B + A − C) ÷ 2
L3 = (C + B − A) ÷ 2
Check: L1 + L2 + L3
= (A + B + C) ÷ 2
R20 = Rt ÷ k
k = 1 + 0.00393 × (t − 20)
Deviation = (R20 − F) ÷ F × 100
F is the factory value. Within 2% passes.

pages.name: Do you still have it?
pages.task: Three loop readings on one cable: L1 to L2, A = 76.90 mΩ. L2 to L3, B = 80.49 mΩ. L3 to L1, C = 81.16 mΩ. What is L1?
pages.alt: Each loop is two cores in series. L1 = (A + C − B) ÷ 2 = (76.90 + 81.16 − 80.49) ÷ 2 = 77.57 ÷ 2 = 38.785 mΩ. 38.115 mΩ comes from L2's formula, and 38.45 mΩ is half of loop A.
pages.html:
Each loop is two cores in series.

L1 = (A + C − B) ÷ 2 = (76.90 + 81.16 − 80.49) ÷ 2 = 77.57 ÷ 2 = 38.785 mΩ.

38.115 mΩ comes from L2's formula, and 38.45 mΩ is half of loop A.

pages.name: What it is for
pages.text: Phase ID makes sure L1, L2 and L3 are identified, labelled and terminated in the right order. Core resistance proves each conductor end to end, its joints and terminations included. Corrected to 20 °C, each core should be within 2% of its factory value. With L1 joined to the screen at B01, only L1 reads continuity at the OSS. So the core marked red at one end is the core marked red at the other.
pages.alt: If it is skipped Phases terminated in the wrong order can give a short when the cable is energised. A poor joint or termination goes unseen. PHASE ID Assume this order. Every core starts earthed at both ends, with a technician at each end. Each core is tested in turn to the screen, from both ends. The far end keeps one core joined to the screen. Under control, it lifts the other two earths. Your end lifts its earths and tests each core to the screen. Only the joined core reads continuity. Then the earths go back on. The two ends then swap jobs and repeat.
pages.html:
If it is skipped

Phases terminated in the wrong order can give a short when the cable is energised. A poor joint or termination goes unseen.

Phase ID

Assume this order. Every core starts earthed at both ends, with a technician at each end. Each core is tested in turn to the screen, from both ends.

The far end keeps one core joined to the screen. Under control, it lifts the other two earths. Your end lifts its earths and tests each core to the screen. Only the joined core reads continuity. Then the earths go back on. The two ends then swap jobs and repeat.

The colours are red L1, yellow L2 and blue L3.

With L1 joined to the screen at B01, only L1 reads continuity at the OSS. L2 and L3 read open. So the core marked red at the OSS is the core marked red at B01.

pages.name: The why
pages.text: Two wires read 429.31 mΩ, 26.52% high. Both leads and both contacts carry the current inside the measured stretch. P probes clipped on the C clamps leave the leads out, but the contacts still add 8.84%. P probes inside the C clamps, facing each other, read the loop alone: 339.31 mΩ.
pages.alt: Low resistance usually means under 1 Ω. Down there, the test leads and their contacts can add a big share of what you read. A meter works out resistance as the voltage it sees divided by the current it sends. On two wires, the same leads do both jobs. The current runs through each lead and each contact, and each drops a little voltage. The meter adds those drops to the core's own. Four wires split the jobs. The C leads carry the current, but the meter does not measure across them. The meter measures the voltage on the P leads, but almost no current flows in them.
pages.html:
Low resistance usually means under 1 Ω. Down there, the test leads and their contacts can add a big share of what you read.

A meter works out resistance as the voltage it sees divided by the current it sends. On two wires, the same leads do both jobs. The current runs through each lead and each contact, and each drops a little voltage. The meter adds those drops to the core's own.

Four wires split the jobs. The C leads carry the current, but the meter does not measure across them. The meter measures the voltage on the P leads, but almost no current flows in them. So neither the P leads nor their contacts drop any voltage worth counting. The reading is whatever carries the current between the two P points.

Step from two wires to four, then move the P probes inside the C clamps.

Loop A of String B is two cores linked at B01, drawn as one resistor. The loop, lead and contact values are practice values.

Meter reads339.31 mΩ
Above the loop0.00%

With the P probes inside the C clamps, facing each other, only the loop carries current between them. The meter reads the loop alone, 339.31 mΩ.

P on the C clamps still reads 8.84% high. That is far more than the 2% a core is allowed.

pages.name: Check
pages.task: You measure loop A, 339.31 mΩ, with four wires. Then you swap all four 5 m leads for 30 m ones, so the meter can sit further back. What does the reading do?
pages.alt: Almost no current flows in the P leads, so 30 m of P lead drops almost no voltage. The C leads carry the current, but the meter does not measure across them. So the reading holds.
options: It rises by the extra lead resistance
It rises by the extra C lead resistance only
pages.html: Almost no current flows in the P leads, so 30 m of P lead drops almost no voltage. The C leads carry the current, but the meter does not measure across them. So the reading holds.

pages.name: Three loops, three cores
pages.text: Loop A links L1 and L2 at B01, so it reads L1 + L2. Loop B reads L2 + L3, and loop C reads L1 + L3. So L1 = (A + C − B) ÷ 2, L2 = (B + A − C) ÷ 2 and L3 = (C + B − A) ÷ 2. With the worked example's readings, A + B + C = 238.55 mΩ, twice the three cores together.
pages.alt: Your leads cannot reach both ends of a 2.40 km core. So the far end links two cores, and you read the loop they make. Each loop is two cores in series: A = L1 + L2, B = L2 + L3 and C = L1 + L3. Add A and C, and you have L1 twice, plus L2 and L3 once each. Take B away, and L2 and L3 cancel. So L1 = (A + C − B) ÷ 2. L2 = (B + A − C) ÷ 2 and L3 = (C + B − A) ÷ 2 follow the same way. Add all three loops and every core appears twice. So A + B + C = 2 × (L1 + L2 + L3), a quick check on your sums. The link at B01 and its contacts sit between your P points in every loop.
pages.html:
Your leads cannot reach both ends of a 2.40 km core. So the far end links two cores, and you read the loop they make. Each loop is two cores in series: A = L1 + L2, B = L2 + L3 and C = L1 + L3.

Add A and C, and you have L1 twice, plus L2 and L3 once each. Take B away, and L2 and L3 cancel. So L1 = (A + C − B) ÷ 2. L2 = (B + A − C) ÷ 2 and L3 = (C + B − A) ÷ 2 follow the same way.

Add all three loops and every core appears twice. So A + B + C = 2 × (L1 + L2 + L3), a quick check on your sums.

The link at B01 and its contacts sit between your P points in every loop. Four wires at the OSS cannot leave them out. So each core you work out carries half the link. Fit it short, firm and clean.

Step through the three loops.

String B's 2.40 km is a practice value.

L1 = (A + C − B) ÷ 2

L2 = (B + A − C) ÷ 2

L3 = (C + B − A) ÷ 2

Each loop holds two cores, and each core sits in two loops. So A + B + C counts every core twice: 238.55 mΩ is twice the three cores together.

pages.name: Worked example
pages.text: The loops read A = 76.90, B = 80.49 and C = 81.16 mΩ. L1 = 38.785 mΩ, L2 = 38.115 mΩ and L3 = 42.375 mΩ. They add to 119.275 mΩ, half of A + B + C. L3 sits 9.26% above L1 and 11.18% above L2. Explain a gap like that before you submit.
pages.alt: THE LOOPS: A = 76.90, B = 80.49 AND C = 81.16 MΩ L1 = (76.90 + 81.16 − 80.49) ÷ 2 = 77.57 ÷ 2 = 38.785 mΩ. L2 = (80.49 + 76.90 − 81.16) ÷ 2 = 76.23 ÷ 2 = 38.115 mΩ. L3 = (81.16 + 80.49 − 76.90) ÷ 2 = 84.75 ÷ 2 = 42.375 mΩ. Check: (76.90 + 80.49 + 81.16) ÷ 2 = 238.55 ÷ 2 = 119.275 mΩ. And 38.785 + 38.115 + 42.375 = 119.275 mΩ. Name each result by its core, never by a loop letter. L3 reads 9.26% above L1 and 11.18% above L2. Three cores of one cable have the same size and length, so they should read close together. Find out why before you submit a gap like this.

pages.name: A cold cable reads low
pages.text: L1's factory value is 174.70 mΩ at 20 °C. At 12 °C the same sound core reads 169.21 mΩ, 3.14% low and outside 2%. Divide by 1 + 0.00393 × (12 − 20) = 0.96856 and it is back to 174.70 mΩ. About 5 °C either side of 20 °C uses up the whole 2%.
pages.alt: Copper's resistance rises as it warms, by 0.00393 of its 20 °C value for each degree. That is about 0.4% per °C. Factory values are given at 20 °C. So a cable on the seabed at 12 °C reads low, even when it is sound. Correct the reading to 20 °C before you compare it: R20 = Rt ÷ (1 + 0.00393 × (t − 20)). t = 12 °C within 2% 20 °C R20, certificate at 20 °C Rt, DLRO reads at 12 °C 160 165 170 175 180 185 Core resistance (mΩ) L1's certificate value, 174.70 mΩ, is a practice value. DLRO reads 169.21 mΩ Against the certificate −3.14% At 12 °C the cold core reads 169.21 mΩ, 3.14% low.

pages.name: Section B
pages.task: Explain why the P probes must sit inside the C clamps, facing each other.
pages.why: A model answer: Below 1 Ω, the leads and their contacts can add as much resistance as the core itself. So a two-wire reading can be well out. A four-wire meter splits the jobs. The test current flows through the C leads, and the voltage is measured on the separate P leads. Almost no current flows in the P leads. So their resistance and their contacts' resistance drop almost no voltage. They do not affect the reading. The meter reads the resistance between the two P points. So the P probes go inside the C clamps, facing each other. Then only the core lies between them, and the C clamps' contact resistance is left outside.

pages.name: Changed numbers
pages.task: Another three-core cable is read at 20 °C, so no correction is needed. Its loops: L1 to L2, A = 120.40 mΩ. L2 to L3, B = 121.10 mΩ. L1 to L3, C = 120.90 mΩ. Determine the resistance of core L3.
pages.alt: Same method, new numbers. These are practice values. Give it in mΩ, to 2 places. L3 = (C + B − A) ÷ 2 = (120.90 + 121.10 − 120.40) ÷ 2 = 121.60 ÷ 2 = 60.80 mΩ Check: (120.40 + 121.10 + 120.90) ÷ 2 = 181.20 mΩ. The three cores, 60.10, 60.30 and 60.80 mΩ, add to the same.
pages.html:
Same method, new numbers. These are practice values. Give it in mΩ, to 2 places.

L3 = (C + B − A) ÷ 2 = (120.90 + 121.10 − 120.40) ÷ 2 = 121.60 ÷ 2 = 60.80 mΩ

Check: (120.40 + 121.10 + 120.90) ÷ 2 = 181.20 mΩ. The three cores, 60.10, 60.30 and 60.80 mΩ, add to the same.
